questions.question: A bar graph shows data as what?
questions.explain: A bar graph uses tall bars side by side so you can see which is biggest. A jumbled list or a page with no labels does not let you compare them that way.

questions.question: A table shows data how?
questions.explain: A table puts data in neat rows and columns so you can read exact numbers. A jumbled list does not organize the data the same way.

questions.question: You have 4 colours and 2 to 5 kids for each. You want to use a picture for every kid. Which display is that?
questions.explain: A pictograph uses a picture for each count, so one star can stand for one kid. A bar graph uses bars and a table uses rows and columns, not pictures.

questions.question: You want to compare 4 colours and see which bar is longest. Which display fits?
questions.explain: A bar graph with labels lets you see the bars next to each other and spot the longest one. A jumbled list or a page with no title does not show the comparison clearly.

questions.question: Sam has a table with 5 pets and the number of kids who picked each. He wants kids to see which pet won at a glance. What should he make next?
questions.explain: A bar graph with a title and labels lets kids see at a glance which pet has the tallest bar. A jumbled list or a graph with no labels does not help them compare.

questions.question: A teacher has exact counts for 3 subjects and wants a simple record in her notebook. Which is the simplest fit?
options: A bar graph with no labels
questions.explain: A table with rows and columns is the simplest way to keep exact numbers in a notebook. A jumbled list is hard to read, and a bar graph with no labels is confusing.

questions.question: You have 6 snacks with 2 to 5 votes each. You want kids to count pictures to see the total. Why does a pictograph work well here?
options: A list would look the same
questions.explain: When each picture stands for one vote, kids can count the pictures to find the total. A jumbled list does not make the counts as easy to see, and a pictograph still needs a key.

questions.question: Tom made a bar graph of 4 sports. He left off the title and the sport names on each bar. His friend says, 'It looks fine, I can read it.' What went wrong?
options: A list would work just as well
A table is always the wrong pick
A bar graph never needs a title
The bars need names and a title
questions.explain: Without labels, you cannot tell which bar is which sport, so the graph is confusing. A jumbled list does not solve the problem, and a bar graph does need a title.

questions.question: You measured 3 plants: 3 cm, 7 cm, and 12 cm. You want to show how much taller each is. A table gives the numbers. What display adds a visual comparison?
options: A bar graph with title and labels
A jumbled list of the plant names
A page with no labels and no title
One number for all three plants
questions.explain: A bar graph with a title and labels shows the three heights as bars you can compare. A jumbled list or a page with no labels does not show the visual difference.

questions.question: Maya wrote down the rainy days for 4 months. She wants her class to see the rainiest month right away. What should she make?
options: A bar graph with no title
questions.explain: A bar graph lets you spot the tallest bar right away. A long list makes you read every number again to compare.

questions.question: Jayden counts the bikes in the school rack each day for 5 days. He wants to write each day's exact count neatly as he counts. What should he use?
options: A bar graph with no labels
A table of day and count
A drawing of the bike rack
questions.explain: A table keeps each day right beside its own exact number. A messy list is easy to mix up or lose track of.

questions.question: Mr. Lee's class counted 4 kinds of pets. He wants the Kindergarten class to read the data by counting pictures. Which display fits best?
options: A long list of pet names
questions.explain: A pictograph lets young kids count pictures instead of reading numbers. It still needs a title and a name for each row.

questions.question: Sofia drew a bar graph of votes for 4 juice flavours. Now she wants to hang it in the hall. What must she add?
options: A list of every single vote
questions.explain: A graph needs a title and a name for each bar so others know what it shows. Bars alone never tell you what was counted.

questions.question: Emma has the rainy day counts for 5 months in her notebook. Her poster must show the exact numbers and also let people compare fast. What should she put on it?
options: A long list of the counts
A table and a bar graph
A bar graph with no months
questions.explain: The table gives the exact numbers and the bar graph makes comparing easy, so both belong on the poster. One long list does neither job well.

questions.question: Zoe's class read 40, 50 and 60 books. She began a pictograph with one book picture for each book and ran out of room. What should she make instead?
options: A list of all book names
A bar graph with a title
questions.explain: With counts this big, one picture for each book takes forever, so bars show the amounts faster. Drawing even more pictures is not a fix.

questions.question: A class wants to record how many books each of 25 kids read. They need to look up every exact number later. Which display fits best?
options: A table of name and count
questions.explain: A table keeps every name next to its own exact number, so any number is easy to find. A long list or 25 crowded bars is hard to read.

questions.question: Ryan wrote all the votes in one long line of words. He says you can spot the winner as fast as with a graph. What went wrong?
options: A list makes you recount to compare
Nothing, his long list is just as clear
Nothing, only the title is missing
He should have written the words neater
questions.explain: In a list you must read and count again to compare, but a graph shows the biggest at a glance. Even a neat list is slow to compare.
